etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English allouance, from Old French alouance.

Morphologically allow +‎ -ance.

quote.citation: 1613 (date written), William Shakespeare, [John Fletcher], “The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eight”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: you sent a large commission to Gregory de Cassado, to conclude, without the King's will or the state's allowance

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: The censure of the which one must in your allowance overweigh a whole theater of others.

definitions.definition: An amount, portion, or share that is allotted or granted; a sum granted as a reimbursement, a bounty, or as appropriate for any purpose

quote.citation: 1847 January – 1848 July, William Makepeace Thackeray, Vanity Fair […], London: Bradbury and Evans […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: Some persons averred that Sir Pitt Crawley gave his brother a handsome allowance.

definitions.definition: Abatement; deduction; the taking into account of mitigating circumstances

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: After making the largest allowance for fraud.

definitions.definition: (commerce) A customary deduction from the gross weight of goods, differing by country.
(horse racing) A permitted reduction in the weight that a racehorse must carry.
(minting) A permissible deviation in the fineness and weight of coins, owing to the difficulty in securing exact conformity to the standard prescribed by law.

quote.text: […] gave allowance where he needed none

quote.citation: 1695, John Locke, The Reasonableness of Christianity:

definitions.definition: (engineering) A planned deviation between an exact dimension and a nominal or theoretical dimension.
(transitive) To put upon a fixed allowance (especially of provisions and drink).
(transitive) To supply in a fixed and limited quantity.
